natural_body: 40% discounts raise acquisition and revenue but hurt retention and renewals.

first.rationale: The two observed declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are sequential stages of the same self-serve funnel, and onboarding is upstream of activation, so a fix there can plausibly recover both; memory_86 and memory_31 both point at that lever. I am spending the verification budget on memory_86 (the direct basis for the intended action) and memory_91 (the strongest alternative, activation_messaging, which targets the larger single drop) because those two are the ones whose original effect sizes and populations would actually change my choice. I deliberately did not verify memory_31: it is the oldest record (day 12) and its claimed 'durable' SMB lift is the most likely to have decayed, but even if it holds it only reinforces a direction I am already taking, so it is low information per analyst hour. Promotional_pricing is the tempting response to the competitor's entry pricing and would likely show a strong short-run acquisition number, but memory_73 records that 40% discounts damage retention and renewals — that is a direct conflict with the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and running it would also contaminate the next few quarters of cohort data used to judge everything else. Enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) and referral_incentive (memory_57) are credible but address neither of the two metrics that actually moved this quarter. Caveats I am carrying forward rather than resolving: every inherited memory is an archived summary, the competitor launch is a genuine regime change that may mean the declines are demand-mix rather than funnel friction (in which case a funnel fix underperforms its historical effect size), and memory_86/memory_31 were measured in a pre-competitor market. Hence standard_experiment with a real control rather than a broad rollout — I want a clean read on whether the historical lift still transfers before committing further slots.
